dct_description_sm: Mercury is a priority contaminant due to its prevalence in the Arctic and high levels found in some traditional food species. Most mercury in the environment is in an inorganic form whereas organic methylmercury (MeHg) is the much more toxic species that biomagnifies through food webs. Processes regulating the standing pool of methylmercury such as inorganic mercury methylation and methylmercury degradation are therefore critical in controlling how much enters aquatic food webs. In 2010 and 2011, this project focused on key production and loss processes for methylmercury in lakes and wetlands on Cornwallis Island and thaw ponds on Bylot Island. The main purpose of this two-year project was to investigate sources and losses of MeHg in Arctic freshwater ecosystems and its uptake in food webs. Project components include: sediment methylation and demethylation rates in lakes and wetlands; characterization of the microbial community involved in methylation and demethylation; photodemethylation rates in the water column and investigation of associated mechanisms; methylmercury in sediment pore water; and methylmercury in lower trophic level components of lake food webs.
dct_title_s: Production and loss of methylmercury, and its uptake in lake food webs of the High Arctic
